title: Narada's equanimity
hook: the great Brahma Narada helps a king back to good sense with calm (Jataka 544)
tomorrow: ten perfections. which one do you need most right now?

segments.voice: Yesterday: upekkha, balance, a rock in the wind through praise and blame. Today the rock has to talk to someone.

Somebody at the dinner table has decided that nothing anyone does really matters, so why bother. You can feel the table getting ready for a fight. An old Jataka starts right there. King Angati takes a teacher's word that deeds bear no fruit: good or bad, nothing comes back. So he stops giving, and lets his duties slide. His daughter, Ruja, pleads with him, and he won't hear it. Then, the story says, the great Brahma Narada comes down from his heaven, dressed as a wandering ascetic, to talk with the king. Not to shout him down. To talk.
screen: `NOTHING MATTERS, SO WHY BOTHER?` → `KING ANGATI STOPS GIVING.` → `RUJA PLEADS.` → `NARADA COMES DOWN TO TALK.`

segments.voice: So, the question: how do you help someone back to good sense? The Jataka's answer is in how Narada talks. In this story he is a great Brahma, a god. He could thunder. He doesn't. He reasons with the king, patiently, shows him where careless deeds lead, and stays level when the king pushes back. And the king comes back to good sense. Tradition tells this as the life in which the Bodhisatta perfected equanimity. Calm helps, because a calm voice leaves the other person room to turn around without losing face. A neighbor tradition says nearly the same thing in one line. The book of Proverbs, in the Hebrew Bible, which Jews and Christians both read: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." That's what they share: the calm voice is the one that gets through. And here's the honest difference. Proverbs roots wisdom in reverence for God: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge," it says near its start. In the Jataka, Narada's calm is a perfection trained over many lives, and what he points the king toward is the fruit of the king's own deeds. One grounds wisdom in God; the other in cause and effect and long practice. Each is whole in its own house.
screen: `A GOD WHO DOESN'T THUNDER.` · `ROOM TO TURN AROUND.` · `PROVERBS: A SOFT ANSWER.` · `REVERENCE FOR GOD; DEEDS AND PRACTICE.` · then, large: `CALM HELPS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring back the last time someone near you was upset. Don't replay the argument. Feel your feet on the floor and your breath going out, and find the voice you'd want to answer with: lower, slower, with room in it.
Narada's equanimity: the great Brahma's level calm, which helped a king back to good sense without a fight.
Keep this one: calm helps, because a soft answer leaves room to turn around. Twenty-nine of thirty.

howItsDone: The Mahanaradakassapa Jataka is among the great birth stories retold and painted in Theravada temples, and Buddhists cultivate equanimity in meditation as one of the four divine abodes.

notes: Mahanaradakassapa Jataka (Jataka 544) paraphrased: King Angati of Videha accepts the naked ascetic Guna's teaching that deeds bear no fruit, stops giving; his daughter Ruja pleads; the Brahma Narada (the Bodhisatta) descends in the guise of an ascetic and, by patient argument and a description of the hells, restores him to right view. Confirm the details used (Ruja, the disguise, 'comes down from his heaven').
'Tradition tells this as the life in which the Bodhisatta perfected equanimity' follows the outline's mapping; confirm.

Unity thread (wisdom day): shared, the calm voice that gets through (Proverbs 15:1, KJV); honest difference, Proverbs roots wisdom in the fear of the LORD (Proverbs 1:7, KJV), while the Jataka grounds Narada's calm in long practice and the fruit of deeds. Ranks neither. A Jewish or Christian reader and a Buddhist Keeper should both confirm the framing is fair. KJV is cited; JPS 1917 wording may differ slightly.
